reason: A standing exclusion for this chapter. 'They which are' is the 1830 text's ordinary relative construction — the 1920 edition rewrote it to 'those who are' at 10:3, 10:16 twice, 10:19, 10:21 and 10:22 — and it will match any KJV verse using the same relative. Romans 9:8, Mark 12:43 ('all they which have', proposed at 10:22) and Luke 8:10 are all instances of this and none is a borrowing. The same applies to 'it must needs be' (Matthew 18:7) and 'and now, behold, the Lord' (Joshua 14:10).

Four words, and the KJV verse is the lying prophet of Bethel: 'an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD... But he lied unto him.' 2 Nephi 10:3's parenthesis is the angel of 2 Nephi 6:9 telling Jacob the Messiah's name. The one KJV verse where an angel speaks to a man in these words is the one where the claim is false, which makes the string match actively misleading rather than merely empty.

Leviticus 26:36 has 'in the lands of their ENEMIES' — the curse of exile; 2 Nephi 10:7 has 'unto the lands of their INHERITANCE' — the promise of return. 'Lands of their inheritance' is in no KJV verse at all, which is why the window closes early (ADJUDICATING 4). Malachi 4:1 ('the day cometh that'), Exodus 10:6 and Galatians 1:16 are proposed at the same verse on connective strings and are covered by the standing exclusion at 10:3.

The top-ranked candidate for the verse and it is a coincidence of five common words. Luke 1:15 is Gabriel on John the Baptist, 'he shall be great in the sight of the Lord'; 2 Nephi 10:8 is 'the nations of the Gentiles shall be great in the eyes of me'. Luke 1:15 is a real source elsewhere in this book (2 Nephi 3:24, on being filled with the Spirit from the womb), which makes the false positive here worth registering rather than passing over. A genuine four-word run whose sense is exactly opposed. Luke 22:25: 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors' — a warning against Gentile rule. 2 Nephi 10:9: 'the kings of the Gentiles shall be nursing fathers unto them' — a promise that Gentile rule will nurse Israel. The verse's source is Isaiah 49:23, where the phrase 'nursing fathers' and 'nursing mothers' are both KJV singletons; 'kings of the Gentiles' is Jacob's own gloss on Isaiah's unspecified 'kings', not a borrowing from Luke.

Five words, and the fifth diverges: Psalm 41:2 has 'blessed upon the EARTH' of the man who considers the poor; 2 Nephi 10:10 has 'blessed upon the LAND', the land being the subject of the whole passage. The construction is ordinary KJV blessing-formula English and points at no particular verse.

Five words of pure land-promise boilerplate. Numbers 32:22 is the Reubenites' conditional possession of Gilead; 2 Nephi 10:11 is the land of liberty. Nothing after the shared string agrees. The theological warrant behind 10:11-14 is 1 Samuel 8, which is linked at 10:11, and 'land of liberty' is in no KJV verse.

Ezekiel 7:27 has 'I will do unto them after their way', a judgment formula; the Book of Mormon's clause is a promise about timing. Common connective phrasing in both.

The string is real but the source is not. The link is written at Galatians 3:28, with 1 Corinthians 12:13 recorded as the source of the substituted first pair.

Five words of comparison boilerplate. Lamentations 1:21 says the enemies 'shall be like unto me' in ruin; 2 Nephi 10:18 says the Gentiles 'shall be like unto a father' to Lehi's seed. Opposite valence, no other contact.

Note the crux recorded there: the verse Jacob is actually expounding, Isaiah 11:11, reads 'islands of the sea' in the KJV and in the Book of Mormon's own transcription at 2 Nephi 21:11 — so the plural he builds an argument on is not the plural his source gives him.

'Cheer up' is a KJV singleton, and the one verse is the newlywed's exemption from military service: 'he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.' 2 Nephi 10:23's 'Therefore cheer up your hearts' has nothing to do with it, and the idiom had passed into ordinary nineteenth-century English by any route. The model case for CONVENTIONS 5's warning that a rarity count is evidence about a phrase, not about a link.

Five words, and the fifth is the hinge. Titus 2:11 is 'the grace of God that BRINGETH SALVATION hath appeared to all men' — grace appearing; 2 Nephi 10:24 is 'the grace of God that YE ARE SAVED' — grace saving. The saving formula is Ephesians 2:8's, 'by grace are ye saved', a KJV singleton in that exact form, and the link is written there. Titus 2:11 remains the machine's best guess for the chapter and is worth recording as a near miss.

A five-word run across the most theologically loaded word in the verse, and it is a coincidence. 2 Samuel 21:3 is David asking the Gibeonites what blood-price will make atonement for Saul's slaughter of them; 2 Nephi 10:25 is a benediction about deliverance from everlasting death 'by the power of the atonement'. The English 'make the atonement, that ye may' and 'the atonement, that ye may' are the same words doing unrelated work. The verse's sources are Philippians 3:10 and 2 Peter 1:3-11.
